question: In a dispute where a Rs.10 lakh business loan was split into two registered mortgages and four promissory notes because stamp duty could not be paid, what security did the borrower furnish at the panchayat held on 24.06.2000 after defaulting on interest under the promissory notes?
answer: At the panchayat dated 24.06.2000 the borrower produced the title document of his property as security for the debt under the four promissory notes, which was recorded in an Agreement of the same date that became the root of the litigation.
gold_passage:
6. Besides the two mortgages supra, the respondent borrowed the remaining Rs.8,50,000/- (Rupees
Eight Lakhs Fifty Thousand) in four promissory notes on different dates. Since there was default in
payment of interest, the appellant demanded repayment of the amount due under the four
promissory notes. The respondent thereupon, in various panchayats, promised to repay the
amounts. Ultimately, in the panchayat dated 24.06.2000, the respondent produced title document
of his property as security towards debt under the four promissory notes, which has been noted in
the Agreement dated 24.06.2000 (hereinafter referred to as the “Agreement”). This Agreement, in
essence, is the root of the instant lis.

answer: The regular appeal, R.A. No.54 of 1977, filed the same day as his Order 9 Rule 13 application, was dismissed on 8.3.1978 as time barred; he then filed the separate suit under Section 9 CPC in 1979 alleging fraud and misrepresentation.
gold_passage:

meantime, Boraiah applied for execution vide Execution Case No.441/77. On 12.1.1979, Patel

question: Did the Supreme Court accept that the twelve-year limitation under Article 136 of the Limitation Act 1963 for executing a final partition decree remains suspended until the decree is engrossed on non-judicial stamp paper, in view of Sections 2(15) and 35 of the Indian Stamp Act 1899?
answer: No; limitation runs from when the decree becomes enforceable and cannot stay suspended at the litigant's volition through delay in furnishing stamp paper, and the Calcutta Special Bench decision in Bholanath Karmakar holding that limitation does not begin until engrossment on stamp paper was overruled.
gold_passage:
Limitation starts by reason of the statutory provisions as prescribed in the statute. Time
does not stop running at the instance of any individual unless, of course, the same has a statutory
sanction being conditional, as more fully noticed hereinbefore: the Special Bench decision of the
Calcutta High Court in the case of Bholanath Karmakarand others v. Madanmohan Karmakar (AIR
1988 Calcutta 1), in our view has completely misread and misapplied the law for the reasons noted
above and thus cannot but be said to be not correctly decided and thus stands overruled.
Undoubtedly, the judgment of the Calcutta High Court has been a very learned judgment but
appreciation of the legislative intent has not been effected in a manner apposite to the intent rather
had a quick shift therefrom by reason wherefor, the Special Bench came to a manifest error in
recording that the period of limitation for execution of a partition decree shall not begin to run until
the decree is engrossed on requisite stamp paper.

question: Where standard rent fixed by a Rent Controller under the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act 1950 was attacked on the ground that the 1956 Tenancy Act's provision continuing pending proceedings under the repealed Act violated Article 14, could that constitutional question be examined in appeals and revisions arising from the Rent Controller's orders?
answer: No; extending the rule applied to taxing statutes, the Court held the question of ultra vires was wholly foreign to the Rent Controller's jurisdiction, so neither the High Court nor the Supreme Court could examine constitutional validity in proceedings arising out of fixation of standard rent.
gold_passage:
In other words it can well be said that the question of ultra vires was
wholly foreign to the scope and the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller. As the appeals and the
revisions which were later preferred were from the orders of the Rent Controller fixing the standard
rent in accordance with the provisions of the Rent Control statute, we are unable to see any
distinction between the present cases and those decided by this Court arising out of a taxing statute.
If the Rent Controller could not have decided the Constitutional validity of the provisions which
have been impugned in the same way as the taxing authorities could not have determined the
Constitutional validity of the taxing statute it would not be open either to the High Court or to this
Court to go into those questions in proceedings arising out of fixation of standard rent.

question: What is the settled position on the Election Commission's powers under Article 324 where the Representation of the People Act 1951 and the Conduct of Election Rules 1961 already prescribe the method of voting by ballot?
answer: The Commission's Article 324 powers supplement rather than supplant the law: it may pass any orders only where legislation and rules are silent, it cannot override the Act or Rules or disobey their mandate, and it cannot implement a direction requiring government approval when that approval is refused, so its order for machine voting was without jurisdiction.
gold_passage:
To sum up, therefore, the legal and constitutional position is as follows:
(a) When there is no Parliamentary legislation or rule made under the said
legislation, the Commission is free to pass any orders in respect of the conduct of
elections.
(b) where there is an Act and express Rules made thereunder it is not open to the
Commission to override the Act or the Rules and pass orders in direct disobedience
to the mandate contained in the Act or the Rules. In other words, the powers of the
Commission are meant to supplement rather than supplant the law (both statute and
Rules) in the matter of superintendence, direction and control as provided by Art.
324,
(c) where the Act or the Rules are silent, the Commission has no doubt plenary
powers under Art.
324 to give any direction in respect of the conduct of election, and
(d) where a particular direction by the Commission is submitted to the government for approval, as
required by the Rules, it is not open to the Commission to go ahead with implementation of it at its
own sweet will even if the approval of the Government is not given.

question: Under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act 1963, can time spent obtaining a certified copy of the judgment before the High Court's refusal of leave to appeal be excluded in computing the 60-day limitation for a special leave petition to the Supreme Court?
answer: No; Section 12(2) only permits exclusion of time caused by an event intervening between the commencement and termination of the limitation period, and has no concern with events anterior to its commencement, so copy-time earned before the refusal of leave cannot be excluded.
gold_passage:
If time taken for obtaining a copy of the order before the commencement of the period of
limitation could be excluded, on the parity of reasoning, time taken for obtaining a copy of the order
after the period of limitation also could he excluded. This would lead to an anomalous position: a
party can keep quiet till the period of limitation has run out and thereafter apply for a certified copy
of the order and claim to exclude the time taken for obtaining the certified copy of the order from
the period of limitation. That could not have been the intention of the Legislature. The object of the
Legislature, therefore, was to enable a party to exclude the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the
order alter the period of limitation has commenced. The phraseology used in Sub-section (2) of
Section 12 of the Limitation Act carries out that object. We, therefore, hold that the petitioner
cannot exclude the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the order before the High Court refused to
give leave. The petition is clearly out of time.

question: Under the Criminal Procedure Code 1973, did the Supreme Court uphold a pardon tendered to an approver by the Chief Judicial Magistrate after the Sessions Judge forwarded the pardon application in a murder-robbery case that had already been committed to the Court of Session?
answer: No; once a case is committed, Section 307 vests the power to tender pardon exclusively in the court to which commitment is made, the Chief Judicial Magistrate has no concurrent jurisdiction under Section 306, the defect is not curable under Section 460(g), and the approver's evidence therefore could not be relied upon.
gold_passage:
8. The aforesaid Section has now taken the place of Section 307 in the new Code. This
indicates that in the changed circumstances the legislature thought it necessary to
delete the expression "or order the committing Magistrate or the District Magistrate
to tender a Pardon" from Section 307 of the present Code which was there in Section
338 of the previous Code. On a plain reading of the provisions contained in Sections
306 and 307 of the Code and on examining the changes that have been brought about
by the legislature from the corresponding provisions of the old Code, the conclusion
is irresistible that under the new Procedure Code of 1973 once a case is committed to
the Court of Sessions then it is only that Court to which the proceedings have been
committed can tender pardon to a person and the Chief Judicial Magistrate cannot be
said to have concurrent jurisdiction for tendering pardon.

question: In litigation by parcel porters engaged through contractors at Northern Railway stations who sought regularization, what did the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Lucknow find in the enquiry conducted pursuant to the Supreme Court's directions of 30.11.1992?
answer: He found that the parcel handling work was permanent and perennial in nature and sufficient to keep all the porters continuously engaged, that the requirements of Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 were satisfied, and that the porters had worked continuously for long years without break in service.
gold_passage:
8. Pursuant to the directions given by this Court in the instant case on 30.11.1992, the Assistant
Labour Commissioner (Central) Lucknow conducted an elaborate enquiry and submitted a detailed
report in which he had recorded the findings that the work of parcel handling Northern Railway is
permanent and perennial in nature and sufficient to keep all the Parcel Porters engaged
continuously, and the requirements of Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition)
Act, 1970 had been satisfied and the petitioner parcel porters were working continuously for long
years without any break in service.

question: Where a High Court reversed the acquittals of district agricultural officers accused of certifying fictitious transport of imported fertilisers from Kakinada port, what standard did the Supreme Court apply for basing a conviction on circumstantial evidence?
answer: All the links in the chain of events from which an irresistible conclusion of guilt can be drawn must be established beyond the pale of reasonable doubt, and the court must not allow suspicion to take the place of legal proof; applying this, the officers were acquitted on benefit of doubt for want of proof of the actual stock position.
gold_passage:
It is true that there is no absolute
standard of proof in a criminal trial and the court should not nurture fanciful doubts by exaggerated
devotion to the rule of benefit of doubt but in a case of circumstantial evidence all the links in the
chain of events from which irresistible conclusion about the guilt of the accused for the offence
alleged can be drawn, must be established beyond the pale of reasonable doubt. The court has to be
watchful and avoid the danger of allowing suspicion to take the place of legal proof.

question: In a contempt case over a statement alleging a planned conspiracy to murder during the Kerala Bandh that was published in a newspaper two days after the suspects' arrest, from what point did the Supreme Court hold that proceedings in court became imminent?
answer: Once the accused had been arrested in the serious cognizable murder case, proceedings in court were imminent, so the newspaper editor who published the statement after the arrest was guilty of contempt, while the maker of the statement, who made it before any arrest, was not.
gold_passage:
Let us now examine the case of P. Govinda Pillai, the second appellant. The statement was
published, as we have already said, in the daily newspaper Called "Deshabhimani" on September 25,
1967. Were any proceedings in a court imminent on that date ? The accused had already been
arrested on September 23, 1969, in a serious cognizable case. Arrest means that the police was
prima facie on the right track. The accused must have been produced before a magistrate within 24
hours of the arrest in accordance with Art. 21 of the Constitution, and, the magistrate must have
authorised further detention of the accused. In these circumstances it is difficult to say 'that any
proceedings in a court were not imminent on that date. The fact that the police may have after
investigation come to the conclusion that the accused was innocent does not make the proceedings
any the less imminent.
